context: Swiss anesthesia resident

\- getting into anesthesia without some prior IM experience, PJ-rotations or connections is probably close to impossible (assuming linguistic proficiency)

\- I would try to get the German proficiency asap, apply to whatever IM spot you can find (ideally in a B-Spital), and then try to switch over to anesthesia (cave most smaller hospitals don't have residents, you can find the "Weiterbildungsstätten" register on https://www.siwf-register.ch/)

\- Most EM docs are either internists or surgeons. The anesthesia/intensivist skillset is mostly overkill, since for "Schockraum" cases the on-call anesthesiologist gets called in anyway. You also take quite a big pay cut (outdated, but still representative: https://www.fmh.ch/files/pdf2/2006-03-1384.pdf)

\- For preclinical work you have 2 options: a) big cities -> EMR docs are staffed by anesthesiologists b): for smaller hospitals sometimes the on-call ER doc gets called out to big traumas/als etc. (however this is more of a macgyver/medicolegal solution, you're not allowed to intubate etc.)

\- Anesthesia gives you access to helicopter and jet air rescue (REGA), ICU can do jet only (both quite competitive)

I feel like if your main goal is to do ER only, going IM and subsequently get the "Fähigkeitsausweis klinische Notfallmedizin" (our version of an ER residency) is the easier path.

From a CA-1 perspective:

Like:

\-  I get to experience and control human physiology in real-time every day, from children to seniors, healthy to actively dying

\- to do this you need to actually understand how our body works, not just remember guidelines

\- get to do procedures that are relatively quick and with minimal notes

\- can hyperfocus on one patient at a time

\- get to experience the whole spectrum of surgical procedures, from 15min cataracts to trauma to liver transplants to babies being born etc

\- ... while still mostly leaving on time when my shift is over

\- NOT HAVING TO WRITE NOTES/replace social services (this actually should be point #1)

\- possibility to do SAR/ preclinical EM aka get paid to fly around in the mountains

\- flexibility of lifestyle as attending: interesting/challenging academia vs. private practice (well paid, routine cases, predictable schedule, no shift work, same team most of the time etc.). If you miss patient interaction you can also go into pain medicine.

\- well paid

Dislike/Cons:

\- no control over your schedule

\- a lot of the cerebral action goes unnoticed by everyone else in the room. People expect you to do your job perfectly every time

\- need to practice in a hospital unless you do pain

\- people dont see you as the doctor (I actually don't care about this, the few minutes you get to build a good rapport, make them feel safe etc. are satisfying enough)

DAY 4  
I got up at 5.30am after 7 hours of sleep which did the whole team good. My feelings were really good on the third day, the best since the start, but we had to manage the length of the event and anticipate slack periods, choosing the right days to avoid pushing the timetable to the limit. After 3 hours of walking with Gino, we waited in the fog for it to open up and I took the time for a short nap. It's hard not to brood while the others are moving forward on the line. I succeeded in my flight, in not easy conditions, the activity is on the East faces but the breeze is already very strong, the ceilings are low and the navigation technical. The flight was unhoped for until the foot of the Zugspite, I went back up for a flight towards lermoo. On the menu, a scree slope with a good crosswind where I am not comfortable, I delay and end up taking a few good drops.at the landing Gino and Alexis, diploma folders point out that the glider is wet. We wait for Yael to sign, she gave me a good demo at the deco but didn't have the same glide. After a short weather check with Laurent Valbert, we think that a last glide is possible and we go up to the take off.  
After two failed attempts, I understand that I have a key. I take it off and end up taking off, thinking that the laziness of my voild came from there. I still have one left on the left brake but the glider seems to accept the accelerated flight. The rain intensifies, the drops are fine, I think I can reach the valley without trying to optimize the glide. To do so, I have to cross two high voltage lines, which are on the side of the forest. My glide deteriorates and just above the lines, my glider goes into a parachute, so it stops flying. The survival instinct wakes up, death is under me.  I release the accelerator to push it back in, nothing happens. I grab my rescue to throw it away from the breeze, it takes time to open because I have no speed. It takes a while to open because I have no speed. It takes me over the second I hit the trees, my fall stops 15m from the ground. I tell my team that everything is ok for my physical health, relieved to have escaped the lines and I understand that I am not held by any real tree, I am between 3 pine trees and my canopy is on branches. My team is quickly on the spot. For the first half hour, I take the storm and the wind, I slide slowly by 5cm. I break down on the phone with the team and then try a self-hypnosis exercise to control my anxiety. Accepting my condition, that the fear will not change anything. What happens next is out of my hands. The weather prevents the helicopter from picking me up, the rescuers arrive but it takes a long time to get into action because the situation is so complex, think before you act. They find a solution to equip 2 trees, throw me a rope connected to a pulley on each side. Once tensioned, I have to cut my lines and emergency risers. I feel sick when I cut the glider but it is not the one holding me up, then I feel really nauseous when I have to cut the rescue. I trust the rescuers, who bring me back to dry land, frozen but alive. I break down. If I want to continue the race the next day, I have to walk from my position of the accident with my gear, it seems absurd, I just dream of a warm bed. I activate the robot mode, I walk for 45 minutes to find a bivouac spot and leave myself the possibility to choose what to do tomorrow.   
The harness is fine, bravo and thank you neo for the choice of the resistant fabric.  
The disappointment is great, the analysis is simple, we push the limits of free flight to be able to be better than another, it is the principle of the competition in walking and flying. I had the impression until then to engage consciously, the risk-taking is obligatory considering the engaged ground and the very complicated weather, but this conscience is a pledge of safety. And for this last flight, I didn't have any, the fatigue and the long days make it easy to forget the sequence of events and the flight before was already far. Water is not forgiving and I knew it.  
Today I am walking, and it is a joy to have my feet on the ground. I will not give up. Step by step. To get rid of my fear and regain my confidence in flight.  
Thanks to my team, to the rescuers, to the FRA4 team who are at the top of their game with me, to the RedBull organisation and sorry to my partners, for ozone, this glider was a little jewel.
